claim: The ability to flexibly navigate an environment relies on a hippocampal-dependent cognitive map.
source: The ability to flexibly navigate an environment relies on a hippocampal-dependent cognitive map.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to foundational work (Tolman, 1948; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Epstein et al., 2017) in the introduction.

claim: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with a higher proportion of place cells.
source: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with a higher proportion of place cells, smaller place fields, increased spatial selectivity and stability.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with smaller place fields.
source: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with a higher proportion of place cells, smaller place fields, increased spatial selectivity and stability.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2E showing place field width was significantly decreased in OZ compared to ØZ.

claim: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with increased spatial selectivity.
source: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with a higher proportion of place cells, smaller place fields, increased spatial selectivity and stability.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data showing lower out/in field firing ratios and higher spatial information in the presence of objects (Figure 1J, K).

claim: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with increased stability.
source: Virtual objects enhanced spatial coding resolution in their vicinity with a higher proportion of place cells, smaller place fields, increased spatial selectivity and stability.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data showing significantly higher stability index in OT compared to ØT (Figure 1I).

claim: The effect of virtual objects on spatial coding resolution was highly dynamic upon objects manipulations.
source: This effect was highly dynamic upon objects manipulations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing rapid changes in place cell properties when objects were added or removed.

claim: Objects improved temporal coding resolution through improved theta phase precession.
source: Objects also improved temporal coding resolution through improved theta phase precession and theta timescale spike coordination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7 showing significant phase precession in OT but not ØT.

claim: Objects improved temporal coding resolution through improved theta timescale spike coordination.
source: Objects also improved temporal coding resolution through improved theta phase precession and theta timescale spike coordination.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7F showing strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance in OT but not ØT.

claim: When animals move in their environment, hippocampal place cells fire in specific locations (their place fields).
source: When animals move in their environment, hippocampal place cells fire in specific locations (their place fields) and this spatial tuning is believed to provide a neuronal substrate to the cognitive map.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations and general scientific knowledge.

claim: Hippocampal place cell spatial tuning is believed to provide a neuronal substrate to the cognitive map.
source: When animals move in their environment, hippocampal place cells fire in specific locations (their place fields) and this spatial tuning is believed to provide a neuronal substrate to the cognitive map.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: A dynamic control of hippocampal spatial coding resolution between different regions of the same environment could be important for spatial navigation.
source: A dynamic control of hippocampal spatial coding resolution between different regions of the same environment could be important for spatial navigation (Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Wild animals, including rodents, often travel kilometers away from their home through empty space to specific food locations.
source: Wild animals, including rodents, often travel kilometers away from their home through empty space to specific food locations (Taylor, 1978).
evidence: This is a factual statement about animal behavior supported by a citation.

claim: Mapping all traveled space at similar spatial resolution would require a huge neuronal and computational investment.
source: Mapping all traveled space at similar spatial resolution would require a huge neuronal and computational investment.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on computational considerations.

claim: Mapping different parts of the same environment at different spatial resolutions could be advantageous.
source: Alternatively, mapping different parts of the same environment at different spatial resolutions could be advantageous.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on logical reasoning.

claim: Place cells can code more or less accurately for space depending on passive vs active movements.
source: Qualitatively, place cells can code more or less accurately for space depending on several behavioral/experimental manipulations such as passive vs active movements (Terrazas et al., 2005) or light vs dark conditions (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Place cells can code more or less accurately for space depending on light vs dark conditions.
source: Qualitatively, place cells can code more or less accurately for space depending on several behavioral/experimental manipulations such as passive vs active movements (Terrazas et al., 2005) or light vs dark conditions (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Better accuracy in place cell coding is generally associated with decreased place field size.
source: A better accuracy is generally associated with decreased place field size, increased spatial and temporal place field stability upon repeated visits of the same location and low out-of-field firing rate.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Better accuracy in place cell coding is generally associated with increased spatial and temporal place field stability upon repeated visits of the same location.
source: A better accuracy is generally associated with decreased place field size, increased spatial and temporal place field stability upon repeated visits of the same location and low out-of-field firing rate.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Better accuracy in place cell coding is generally associated with low out-of-field firing rate.
source: A better accuracy is generally associated with decreased place field size, increased spatial and temporal place field stability upon repeated visits of the same location and low out-of-field firing rate.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The number of spatially selective cells can increase globally in the presence of objects.
source: Quantitatively, the number of spatially selective cells and place fields' density can increase globally in the presence of objects (Burke et al., 2011) and locally near rewarded locations (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Hollup et al., 2001; Dupret et al., 2010; Danielson et al., 2016; Gauthier and Tank, 2018; Sato et al., 2018), salient sensory cues (Wiener et al., 1989; Hetherington and Shapiro, 1997; Sato et al., 2018) or connecting parts in multi-compartment environments (Spiers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burke et al., 2011.

claim: Place fields' density can increase locally near rewarded locations.
source: Quantitatively, the number of spatially selective cells and place fields' density can increase globally in the presence of objects (Burke et al., 2011) and locally near rewarded locations (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Hollup et al., 2001; Dupret et al., 2010; Danielson et al., 2016; Gauthier and Tank, 2018; Sato et al., 2018), salient sensory cues (Wiener et al., 1989; Hetherington and Shapiro, 1997; Sato et al., 2018) or connecting parts in multi-compartment environments (Spiers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Place fields' density can increase locally near salient sensory cues.
source: Quantitatively, the number of spatially selective cells and place fields' density can increase globally in the presence of objects (Burke et al., 2011) and locally near rewarded locations (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Hollup et al., 2001; Dupret et al., 2010; Danielson et al., 2016; Gauthier and Tank, 2018; Sato et al., 2018), salient sensory cues (Wiener et al., 1989; Hetherington and Shapiro, 1997; Sato et al., 2018) or connecting parts in multi-compartment environments (Spiers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Place fields' density can increase locally near connecting parts in multi-compartment environments.
source: Quantitatively, the number of spatially selective cells and place fields' density can increase globally in the presence of objects (Burke et al., 2011) and locally near rewarded locations (O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Hollup et al., 2001; Dupret et al., 2010; Danielson et al., 2016; Gauthier and Tank, 2018; Sato et al., 2018), salient sensory cues (Wiener et al., 1989; Hetherington and Shapiro, 1997; Sato et al., 2018) or connecting parts in multi-compartment environments (Spiers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Spiers et al., 2015.

claim: Distal visual cues play an important role in map orientation.
source: While distal visual cues play an important role in map orientation and environmental boundaries in map anchoring (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996; Knierim and Rao, 2003; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011), local sensory cues, with a high sensory resolution, could be instrumental in setting spatial coding resolution (Hartley et al., 2000; Strösslin et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2006; Sheynikhovich et al., 2009; Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Environmental boundaries play an important role in map anchoring.
source: While distal visual cues play an important role in map orientation and environmental boundaries in map anchoring (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996; Knierim and Rao, 2003; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011), local sensory cues, with a high sensory resolution, could be instrumental in setting spatial coding resolution (Hartley et al., 2000; Strösslin et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2006; Sheynikhovich et al., 2009; Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Local sensory cues, with a high sensory resolution, could be instrumental in setting spatial coding resolution.
source: While distal visual cues play an important role in map orientation and environmental boundaries in map anchoring (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996; Knierim and Rao, 2003; Knierim and Hamilton, 2011), local sensory cues, with a high sensory resolution, could be instrumental in setting spatial coding resolution (Hartley et al., 2000; Strösslin et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2006; Sheynikhovich et al., 2009; Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Head-fixed mice were trained to run on a wheel and to shuttle back and forth on a 2 m-long virtual linear track to collect liquid rewards at its extremities.
source: To investigate the effect of local visual cues on hippocampal coding resolution, head-fixed mice were trained to run on a wheel and to shuttle back and forth on a 2 m-long virtual linear track to collect liquid rewards at its extremities (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The lateral walls of the virtual track displayed distinct visual patterns to provide directional information.
source: The lateral walls of the virtual track displayed distinct visual patterns to provide directional information.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Mice were trained either in the presence or absence of 3D visual cues (virtual objects).
source: To investigate the contribution of local cues to hippocampal spatial representation, mice were trained either in the presence or absence of 3D visual cues (hereafter called virtual objects; Objects Track, OT: n = 3 mice; No Objects Track, ØT: n = 3 mice), which were virtually positioned on the floor of the track between the animal trajectory and the walls (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Virtual objects were virtually positioned on the floor of the track between the animal trajectory and the walls.
source: To investigate the contribution of local cues to hippocampal spatial representation, mice were trained either in the presence or absence of 3D visual cues (hereafter called virtual objects; Objects Track, OT: n = 3 mice; No Objects Track, ØT: n = 3 mice), which were virtually positioned on the floor of the track between the animal trajectory and the walls (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The running wheel forced the animals to run in a unidirectional manner.
source: The running wheel forced the animals to run in a unidirectional manner so that they repetitively ran along the virtual objects without the possibility to orient toward them or explore them with any sensory modality but vision.
evidence: This describes a constraint of the experimental setup.

claim: Animals repetitively ran along the virtual objects without the possibility to orient toward them or explore them with any sensory modality but vision.
source: The running wheel forced the animals to run in a unidirectional manner so that they repetitively ran along the virtual objects without the possibility to orient toward them or explore them with any sensory modality but vision.
evidence: This describes a constraint of the experimental setup.

claim: Animals received a reward (sucrose in water 5%) each time they reached one of the extremities of the linear track.
source: Animals received a reward (sucrose in water 5%) each time they reached one of the extremities of the linear track.
evidence: This describes the reward protocol in the experiment.

claim: After licking, the mice were 'teleported' in the same position but facing the opposite direction of the track.
source: After licking, the mice were 'teleported' in the same position but facing the opposite direction of the track (Figure 1C), allowing them to run back and forth in the same environment.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: A total of 1021 neurons were recorded in the CA1 pyramidal cell layer in OT and ØT.
source: A total of 1021 neurons were recorded in the CA1 pyramidal cell layer in OT and ØT (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of neurons recorded.

claim: Mice trained in ØT performed the task with similar proficiency than mice trained in OT, as shown by similar rate of reward collections.
source: Mice trained in ØT performed the task with similar proficiency than mice trained in OT, as shown by similar rate of reward collections (ØT: 1.86 ± 0.31 rewards/minute, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: 1.44 ± 0.12 rewards/minute, n = 8 sessions in three mice; Z = 0.52, p=0.59, two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum (WRS) test; all values expressed as mean ±SEM) and average running speed (ØT: 14.1 ± 2.12 cm/s, n = 9 recording sessions in three mice; OT: 15.3 ± 1.28 cm/s, n = 8 recording sessions in three mice; t15 = −0.47, p=0.64, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Mice trained in ØT had similar average running speed compared to mice trained in OT.
source: Mice trained in ØT performed the task with similar proficiency than mice trained in OT, as shown by similar rate of reward collections (ØT: 1.86 ± 0.31 rewards/minute, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: 1.44 ± 0.12 rewards/minute, n = 8 sessions in three mice; Z = 0.52, p=0.59, two-tailed Wilcoxon rank sum (WRS) test; all values expressed as mean ±SEM) and average running speed (ØT: 14.1 ± 2.12 cm/s, n = 9 recording sessions in three mice; OT: 15.3 ± 1.28 cm/s, n = 8 recording sessions in three mice; t15 = −0.47, p=0.64, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The percentage of track active cells was comparable between the track without and with virtual objects.
source: The percentage of track active cells was comparable between the track without and with virtual objects (ØT: 66.4 ± 5.8%, n = 7 sessions in three mice; OT: 54.6 ± 4.8%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t13 = 1.58, p=0.14, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Only 19% of track active cells had at least one place field (place cells) in the empty track.
source: While only 19% of track active cells had at least one place field (place cells) in the empty track (n = 48 place cells), 71% of track active cells were place cells when virtual objects were present (n = 193 place cells; t13 = −7.3, p<10−5, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 71% of track active cells were place cells when virtual objects were present.
source: While only 19% of track active cells had at least one place field (place cells) in the empty track (n = 48 place cells), 71% of track active cells were place cells when virtual objects were present (n = 193 place cells; t13 = −7.3, p<10−5, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In ØT, place fields were relatively sparse in the middle of the track with a large proportion of them aligned either to the beginning or to the end of the track.
source: In ØT, place fields were relatively sparse in the middle of the track with a large proportion of them aligned either to the beginning or to the end of the track (End-Track fields: 53.1 ± 9.95%, n = 7 sessions in three mice; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the maze with objects, the majority of fields were located in the central part of the track.
source: In the maze with objects, however, the majority of fields were located in the central part of the track (On-Track fields: 79 ± 3.52%; n = 8 sessions in three mice; Z = 2.84, p=0.0045, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Local visual cues can strongly increase the proportion of place cells among active cells notably to code the central part of the maze.
source: These results indicate that local visual cues can strongly increase the proportion of place cells among active cells notably to code the central part of the maze.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There was a small, non-significant, tendency for place field width to be lower in the track with objects.
source: There was a small, non-significant, tendency for place field width (calculated on complete fields) to be lower in the track with objects (ØT: 51.5 ± 3.33 cm, n = 15 place fields; OT: 48.7 ± 1.29 cm, n = 157 place fields; Z = 0.93, p=0.35, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 1G), in agreement with a higher spatial coding resolution.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The spatial dispersion of single-trial detected place fields was significantly reduced in the presence of 3D objects.
source: On the other hand, the spatial dispersion of single-trial detected place fields was significantly reduced in the presence of 3D objects (ØT: 11.9 ± 0.90 cm, n = 48 place cells; OT: 9.70 ± 0.44 cm, n = 193 place cells; Z = 2.56, p=0.01, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The stability index was significantly lower in the track without objects.
source: This stability index was significantly lower in the track without objects (ØT: 0.12 ± 0.01, n = 48 place cells; OT: 0.28 ± 0.01, n = 193 place cells; Z = −6.64, p<10−10, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Local visual cues can improve inter-trial spatial and temporal stability.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that local visual cues can improve inter-trial spatial and temporal stability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on stability.

claim: In the track without objects, place cells increased their firing rate inside the place field but also discharged at high rate outside the field.
source: In the track without objects, place cells increased their firing rate inside the place field (7.44 ± 0.75 Hz, n = 48 place cells) but also discharged at high rate outside the field (5.23 ± 0.62 Hz; Figure 1F and J; ratio: 0.65 ± 0.02).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figures 1F and 1J.

claim: Place cells recorded in the track with objects had comparable firing rates inside the place field but fired significantly less outside the field compared to ØT.
source: In comparison, place cells recorded in the track with objects had comparable firing rates inside the place field (6.80 ± 0.43 Hz, n = 193 place cells; Z = 1.5, p=0.13, two-tailed WRS test) but fired significantly less outside the field (3.79 ± 0.34 Hz; ratio: 0.46 ± 0.01; Figure 1F and J; Z = 5.48, p<10−7, two-tailed WRS test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 1F and 1J.

claim: Spatial information was very low in the track without objects and significantly higher in the presence of objects.
source: Accordingly, spatial information (in bit/spike), a measure independent of place fields' detection (Skaggs et al., 1993) was very low in the track without objects (0.06 ± 0.01 bit/spike, n = 48 place cells) and significantly higher in the presence of objects (0.25 ± 0.02 bit/spike, n = 193 place cells; Z = −5.67, p<10−7, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Local visual cues can strongly enhance the proportion of place cells among active cells and place cell's coding accuracy.
source: Altogether these results indicate that local visual cues can strongly enhance the proportion of place cells among active cells but also place cell's coding accuracy in agreement with an improved spatial coding resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: The distribution of On-Track fields in OT was non-uniform.
source: We first noticed that the distribution of these fields was non-uniform (p=0.017, test of non-uniformity).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The density of place fields was significantly higher in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: The density of place fields was significantly higher in OZ (OZ: 7.31 ± 1.09%/10 cm, n = 12 spatial bins of 10 cm, six in each direction; ØZ: 3.28 ± 0.65%/10 cm, n = 20 spatial bins of 10 cm, 10 in each direction; t30 = −3.38, p=0.002, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: In the maze with objects, place fields were significantly smaller in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: Furthermore, in the maze with objects, place fields were significantly smaller in OZ (42.3 ± 1.43 cm, n = 77 fields) compared to ØZ (54.8 ± 1.89 cm, n = 80 fields; Z = 4.60, p<10−5, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Place field dispersion was significantly reduced in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: Accordingly, place field dispersion was also significantly reduced in OZ (8.33 ± 0.50 cm, n = 130 fields) compared to ØZ (11.8 ± 0.71 cm, n = 90 fields; Z = 3.90, p<10−4, two-tailed WRS test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A local stability index was significantly increased in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: A local stability index (see Materials and methods section) was significantly increased in OZ (0.52 ± 0.02, n = 60 bins of 2 cm, 30 in each direction) compared to ØZ (0.39 ± 0.01, n = 100 bins of 2 cm, 50 in each direction; Z = −5.21, p<10−6, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 2C and 2F.

claim: Spatial information was significantly higher in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: Spatial information was also significantly higher in OZ (0.32 ± 0.03 bit/spike, n = 130 fields) compared to ØZ (0.20 ± 0.03 bit/spike, n = 90 fields; Z = −2.16, p=0.03, two-tailed WRS test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in the out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio between fields located in OZ or ØZ.
source: Finally, we found no significant difference in the out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio between fields located in OZ or ØZ (OZ: 0.46 ± 0.02, n = 130 fields; ØZ: 0.49 ± 0.02, n = 90 fields; Z = 1.03, p=0.30, two-tailed unpaired t test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 3D objects can locally improve spatial coding resolution through a local increase in place field number, a local reduction in place field size, a higher local stability and spatial information content.
source: These results indicate that 3D objects can locally improve spatial coding resolution through a local increase in place field number, a local reduction in place field size, a higher local stability and spatial information content while their effect on the out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio is more global.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on local effects.

claim: The effect of 3D objects on the out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio is more global.
source: These results indicate that 3D objects can locally improve spatial coding resolution through a local increase in place field number, a local reduction in place field size, a higher local stability and spatial information content while their effect on the out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio is more global.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In ØT, place fields were non-uniformly distributed.
source: In this track, place fields were also non-uniformly distributed (p=0; test of non-uniformity) with a higher density of fields at the ends of the track (i.e. End-Track fields; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no significant difference between End-Track and On-Track fields in ØT in terms of out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio.
source: However, we found no significant difference between End-Track and On-Track fields in terms of out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio (End-Track: 0.65 ± 0.02, n = 32 fields; On-Track: 0.62 ± 0.03, n = 31 fields; Z = 0.21, p=0.83, two-tailed WRS test) and stability (End-Track: 0.17 ± 0.01, n = 32 fields; On-Track: 0.15 ± 0.02, n = 31 fields; t61 = 1.14, p=0.26, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between End-Track and On-Track fields in ØT in terms of stability.
source: However, we found no significant difference between End-Track and On-Track fields in terms of out-of-field versus in-field firing ratio (End-Track: 0.65 ± 0.02, n = 32 fields; On-Track: 0.62 ± 0.03, n = 31 fields; Z = 0.21, p=0.83, two-tailed WRS test) and stability (End-Track: 0.17 ± 0.01, n = 32 fields; On-Track: 0.15 ± 0.02, n = 31 fields; t61 = 1.14, p=0.26, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Spatial information was low for both End-Track and On-Track fields in ØT but paradoxically lower for End-Track fields.
source: Spatial information was low for both types of fields but paradoxically lower for End-Track fields (End-Track: 0.04 ± 0.01 bit/spike, n = 32 fields; On-Track: 0.1 ± 0.02 bit/spike, n = 31 fields; Z = −2.66, p=0.008, two-tailed WRS test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Overrepresentation of the ends of the ØT is not associated with increased spatial coding accuracy and is unlikely to represent increased spatial coding resolution at these locations.
source: We conclude that overrepresentation of the ends of the ØT is not associated with increased spatial coding accuracy and is unlikely to represent increased spatial coding resolution at these locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of End-Track fields.

claim: The decoding error across trials was nearly two-fold larger in the track without objects compared to the track with objects.
source: Overall, the effect of objects on hippocampal spatial coding was obvious because the decoding error across trials was nearly two-fold larger in the track without objects compared to the track with objects (ØT: 46.3 ± 0.73 cm, n = 180 trials; OT: 27.1 ± 0.94 cm, n = 249 trials; Z = 13.6, p<10−36, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The decoding accuracy was three fold lower in the empty track compared to the track with objects.
source: Accordingly, the decoding accuracy (van der Meer et al., 2010) was three fold lower in the empty track compared to the track with objects (ØT: 0.017 ± 3.8×10−4, n = 180 trials; OT: 0.048 ± 1.49×10−3, n = 249 trials; chance level 0.01; Z = −15.68, p<10−54, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: Decoding accuracy was positively correlated with sample size in the track with objects but not in the track without objects.
source: Decoding accuracy was positively correlated with sample size in the track with objects but not in the track without objects (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Decoding accuracy was better in OT even if the sample size of active cells used was three time lower than in ØT.
source: Importantly, decoding accuracy was better in OT even if the sample size of active cells used was three time lower than in ØT (to compensate for the three time lower proportion of place cells in this condition; ØT n = 15 vs OT n = 5, Z = −2.26, p=0.02, two-tailed WRS test; ØT n = 30 vs OT n = 10, Z = −2.85, p=0.004, two-tailed WRS test; ØT n = 45 vs OT n = 15, Z = −2.55, p=0.01, two-tailed WRS test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Decoding accuracy was uniformly low in the track without objects.
source: While decoding accuracy was uniformly low in the track without objects (OZ: 0.02 ± 1.48×10−3, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: 0.02 ± 8.98×10−4, n = 50 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −1.64, p=0.1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 3E), it was increased in every part of the track with objects but significantly more in OZ compared to ØZ (OZ: 0.06 ± 0.003, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: 0.04 ± 2.3×10−3, n = 50 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −5.21, p<10−6, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Decoding accuracy was increased in every part of the track with objects but significantly more in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: While decoding accuracy was uniformly low in the track without objects (OZ: 0.02 ± 1.48×10−3, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: 0.02 ± 8.98×10−4, n = 50 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −1.64, p=0.1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 3E), it was increased in every part of the track with objects but significantly more in OZ compared to ØZ (OZ: 0.06 ± 0.003, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: 0.04 ± 2.3×10−3, n = 50 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −5.21, p<10−6, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Local visual cues can globally and locally improve spatial coding accuracy at the population level.
source: We concluded that local visual cues can globally and locally improve spatial coding accuracy at the population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis.

claim: Place cells usually appear instantaneously upon exploration of a new environment in area CA1.
source: Place cells usually appear instantaneously upon exploration of a new environment in area CA1 (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Epsztein et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: For mice trained in an empty track, adding objects instantaneously increased the proportion of place cells.
source: For mice trained in an empty track, adding objects instantaneously increased the proportion of place cells (from 21.6 ± 5.3% to 75.0 ± 4.1%; n = 5 sessions in three mice; t4 = −35.8, p<10−5, two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: A large proportion of cells initially silent or active but nonspatially modulated in the familiar empty track became spatially modulated when objects were added.
source: Thus, a large proportion of cells initially silent or active but nonspatially modulated in the familiar empty track became spatially modulated (40.3%).
evidence: This is derived from the data on place cell proportions.

claim: Most of the newly spatially modulated cells had on-track fields.
source: Most of these cells had on-track fields (81.3%; Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: A majority of cells initially spatially modulated remained place cells when objects were added.
source: A majority of cells initially spatially modulated remained place cells (75.7%), while the others became nonspatially modulated or silent.
evidence: This is derived from the data on place cell stability.

claim: Adding objects increased place cells' stability.
source: Adding objects also increased place cells' stability (Z = −4.68, p<10−5, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4E) and spatial information (Z = −3.20, p=0.0014, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Adding objects increased place cells' spatial information.
source: Adding objects also increased place cells' stability (Z = −4.68, p<10−5, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4E) and spatial information (Z = −3.20, p=0.0014, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Local stability was significantly higher in OZ when objects were added but not before.
source: Local stability was significantly higher in OZ when objects were added (OZ: 0.56 ± 0.02, n = 60 bins of 2 cm, 30 in each direction; ØZ: 0.25 ± 0.02, n = 100 bins of 2 cm, 50 in each direction; Z = −8.57, p<10−16, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4I) but not before (Z = 1.25, p=0.21, two-tailed WRS test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Place fields' spatial dispersion was decreased when objects were added.
source: Place fields' spatial dispersion and out/in field firing ratio were decreased (Z = 3.55, p=0.0004 and Z = 1.87, p=0.06, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: Out/in field firing ratio was decreased when objects were added.
source: Place fields' spatial dispersion and out/in field firing ratio were decreased (Z = 3.55, p=0.0004 and Z = 1.87, p=0.06, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: Removing objects decreased the proportion of place cells.
source: On the other hand, removing objects decreased the proportion of place cells (from 71.1 ± 5.54% to 34.9 ± 10.9%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t5 = 5.54, p=0.001, two-tailed paired t-test; Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Removing objects decreased the spatial information and stability.
source: The spatial information and stability were decreased by this manipulation (Z = 2.27, p=0.02 and Z = 4.51, p<10−5, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4E and G), while place field out/in field firing ratio and dispersion were increased (Z = −2.01, p=0.04 and Z = −3.06, p=0.002, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4E and 4G.

claim: Removing objects increased place field out/in field firing ratio and dispersion.
source: The spatial information and stability were decreased by this manipulation (Z = 2.27, p=0.02 and Z = 4.51, p<10−5, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4E and G), while place field out/in field firing ratio and dispersion were increased (Z = −2.01, p=0.04 and Z = −3.06, p=0.002, respectively, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4D and F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claim: After object removal, local stability was not significantly higher in OZ compared to ØZ.
source: After object removal, local stability was not significantly higher in OZ (OZ: 0.24 ± 0.02, n = 60 bins of 2 cm, 30 in each direction) compared to ØZ (0.24 ± 0.02, n = 100 bins of 2 cm, 50 in each direction; Z = 0.19, p=0.85, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The effects of local visual cues on place cells' coding observed between familiar tracks can be reproduced with instantaneous objects manipulation.
source: We conclude that the effects of local visual cues on place cells' coding observed between familiar tracks can be reproduced with instantaneous objects manipulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the objects manipulation experiments.

claim: When objects were added in the empty track, map similarity was significantly higher for the second trial in the new condition.
source: When objects were added in the empty track, map similarity was significantly higher for the second trial in the new condition (t-1 vs t + 2, n = 598 and n = 608 pyramidal cells, respectively; n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = 7.18, p<10−9; Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) and then stayed higher from this second trial on (t + 2 vs t + 3, n = 608 and n = 612 pyramidal cells, respectively; n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = 1.10, p=1, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: When objects were removed from the familiar track with objects, map similarity dropped already for the first trial in the new condition.
source: Conversely, when objects were removed from the familiar track with objects, map similarity dropped already for the first trial in the new condition (t-1 vs t + 1, n = 744 and n = 743 pyramidal cells, respectively; n = 8 sessions in three mice; Z = 8.80, p<10−15, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) and stayed lower from this first trial on (t + 1 vs t + 2, n = 743 and n = 720 pyramidal cells, respectively; Z = 0.17, p=1, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hippocampus can rapidly adapt its spatial coding resolution to local visual cues available in the environment.
source: Thus, the hippocampus can rapidly adapt its spatial coding resolution to local visual cues available in the environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dynamic analysis of map similarity.

claim: Object-responsive cells tend to discharge systematically near several objects present in the environment.
source: Newly activated place cells in OT could correspond to object responsive (OR) cells, which have been recorded in the hippocampus of freely moving rats (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013). These cells tend to discharge systematically near several objects present in the environment.
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: In the track without objects no OR cell was detected.
source: In the track without objects no OR cell was detected.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: In the track with objects, OR cells represented only 2.07% of all place cells.
source: In the track with objects, OR cells represented only 2.07% of all place cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results.

claim: The vast majority of newly activated place cells in the presence of objects does not correspond to OR cells.
source: We conclude that the vast majority of newly activated place cells in the presence of objects does not correspond to OR cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OR cell analysis.

claim: The percentage of active cells was not affected by the presence of different patterns along the track.
source: The percentage of active cells was not affected by the presence of different patterns along the track (OT, 54.64 ± 4.79%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; PØT, 53.63 ± 3.45%, n = 6 sessions in two mice; p=1, one-way Anova test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The percentage of place cells among active cells tended to be greater in PØT than in ØT.
source: The percentage of place cells among active cells tended to be greater than in ØT (ØT, 18.71 ± 4.33%, n = 7 sessions in three mice; PØT, 42.16 ± 10.58%, n = 5 sessions in two mice; p=0.093, one-way Anova test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing a trend.

claim: The percentage of place cells in PØT was significantly lower than in OT.
source: Also, the percentage of place cells in PØT was significantly lower than in OT (OT, 71.11 ± 5.54%, n = 8 sessions in three mice; p=0.024, one-way Anova test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: Place fields were uniformly distributed along the track enriched with patterns.
source: Interestingly, place fields were uniformly distributed along the track enriched with patterns (n = 16 spatial bins of 10 cm; p=0.23, test for non-uniformity; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Local 2D visual cues are sufficient to set place fields' position.
source: This suggests that local 2D visual cues are sufficient to set place fields' position.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the uniform distribution of place fields in PØT.

claim: Place field width was significantly decreased in PØT compared to ØT.
source: Place field width was significantly decreased in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 51.46 ± 3.34 cm, n = 15 place fields; PØT, 41.51 ± 1.17 cm, n = 138 place fields; Z = 2.62, p=0.026, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Place field dispersion was significantly reduced in PØT compared to ØT to a level comparable to OT.
source: Accordingly, place field dispersion was significantly reduced compared to ØT to a level comparable to OT (ØT, 5.95 ± 0.45 cm, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 4.57 ± 0.21 cm, n = 157 place cells; Z = 2.88, p=0.011, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Inter-trial firing stability was significantly higher in PØT compared to ØT but significantly lower than in OT.
source: Inter-trial firing stability, while significantly higher in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 0.12 ± 0.01, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 0.19 ± 0.01, n = 157 place cells; Z = 3.72, p=0.0005, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction), was significantly lower than in OT (OT, 0.28 ± 0.01, n = 193 place cells; Z = 5.02, p<10−4, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Local 2D visual cues can improve place fields stability to a certain extend without reaching the level of stability observed in the presence of 3D virtual objects.
source: We conclude that local 2D visual cues can improve place fields stability to a certain extend without, however, reaching the level of stability observed in the presence of 3D virtual objects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of PØT with ØT and OT.

claim: The ratio of place cells' out-of-field versus in-field firing was lower in PØT compared to ØT but still significantly higher than in OT.
source: The ratio of place cells' out-of-field versus in-field firing was lower in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 0.65 ± 0.02, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 0.53 ± 0.02 cm, n = 157 place cells; Z = 3.38, p=0.002, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) but still significantly higher than in OT (OT, 0.46 ± 0.01, n = 193 place cells; Z = 3.02, p=0.007, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Spatial information content was higher in PØT compared to ØT but still significantly lower than in OT.
source: Accordingly, spatial information content was higher in PØT compared to ØT (ØT, 0.056 ± 0.01, n = 48 place cells; PØT, 0.16 ± 0.02, n = 157 place cells; Z = 4.09, p=0.0001, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction) but still significantly lower than in OT (OT, 0.25 ± 0.02, n = 193 place cells; Z = 2.73, p=0.018, Kruskall-Wallis one-way test with post-hoc Bonferroni correction; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Local 2D visual cues can enhance the proportion of place cells among active cells and place cells' coding accuracy but to a lower extend compared to 3D virtual objects.
source: Altogether these results indicate that local 2D visual cues can enhance the proportion of place cells among active cells and place cells' coding accuracy but to a lower extend compared to 3D virtual objects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of PØT with ØT and OT.

claim: Local stability in OZ was significantly higher in OT compared to PØT.
source: Finally, local stability in OZ was significantly higher in OT compared to PØT (OT-OZ: 0.52 ± 0.02; PØT-OZ: 0.39 ± 0.016, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm for both; Z = 4.85, p<10−5 two-tailed WRS test; Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Decoding accuracy in OZ was significantly higher in OT compared to PØT.
source: Accordingly, the same effect could be observed for the decoding accuracy (OT-OZ: 0.07 ± 0.02; PØT-OZ: 0.03 ± 0.01, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm for both; Z = −5.83, p<10−8 two-tailed WRS test; Figure 5J) in agreement with a strong influence of 3D objects on spatial coding resolution.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The percentage of active cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment.
source: The percentage of active cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = −0.1, p=1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6C) nor was the percentage of place cells (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; t8 = −1.38, p=0.20, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The percentage of place cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment.
source: The percentage of active cells was not increased by visually enriching the environment (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; Z = −0.1, p=1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6C) nor was the percentage of place cells (OT, n = 5 sessions in two mice; EOT, n = 5 sessions in three mice; t8 = −1.38, p=0.20, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 6B-D.

claim: Place fields were uniformly distributed along the track in the visually rich environment.
source: However, place fields were uniformly distributed along the track in the visually rich environment (n = 16 spatial bins of 10 cm; p=0.23, test for non-uniformity), thus not clustered around objects as in the visually poor environment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Local visual cues are important to set place fields' position.
source: This suggests that local visual cues are important to set place fields' position (Renaudineau et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: All other attributes of place fields were not significantly different between OT and EOT.
source: However, all other attributes of place fields were not significantly different between the two environments (OT, n = 103 place cells; EOT, n = 132 place cells; out/in field firing ratio: Z = 0.57, p=0.57; Spatial info: Z = 0.42, p=0.67; Dispersion: Z = −1.88, p=0.06; Stability: Z = −0.06, p=0.95; two-tailed WRS test for all; Figure 6E–H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 6E-H.

claim: There was still a significant effect of objects in the visually enriched environment in OZ versus ØZ in terms of local stability.
source: When looking at local stability of firing rates, we still observed a significant effect of objects in the visually enriched environment in OZ versus ØZ (OZ, n = 60 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: n = 100 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −2.46, p=0.014, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Positions near objects were decoded with a better accuracy than positions further away in the visually enriched environment.
source: Interestingly, positions near objects were also decoded with a better accuracy using a Bayesian decoder than positions further away in the visually enriched environment (OZ: 0.07 ± 0.004, n = 30 spatial bins of 2 cm; ØZ: 0.057 ± 0.003, n = 50 spatial bins of 2 cm; Z = −4.49, p=0.004, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6J.

claim: In the presence of local visual cues, hippocampal spatial coding is not further improved by visually enriching the environment.
source: Altogether these results suggest that in the presence of local visual cues, hippocampal spatial coding is not further improved by visually enriching the environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of OT and EOT.

claim: Place fields locations are influenced by additional visual cues along the track.
source: However, place fields locations are influenced by additional visual cues along the track.
evidence: This is inferred from the uniform distribution of place fields in EOT.

claim: Despite a homogeneous distribution of place field locations, 3D objects could still locally influence hippocampal population decoding accuracy.
source: Interestingly, despite a homogeneous distribution of place field locations, 3D objects could still locally influence hippocampal population decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis in EOT.

claim: Theta phase precession is thought to further increase spatial coding resolution.
source: This phenomenon, called theta phase precession, is thought to further increase spatial coding resolution because different locations within the place field that are difficult to distinguish based on firing rate alone can be accurately separated when phase is taken into account.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Increased spatial resolution in the temporal domain would correspond to increased slope of the phase versus position relationship for identical field sizes.
source: In the temporal domain, increased spatial resolution would thus correspond to increased slope of the phase versus position relationship for identical field sizes.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what increased temporal resolution would entail.

claim: The mean frequency of the field theta oscillation was not significantly different when mice were running in the track with or without objects.
source: The mean frequency of the field theta oscillation was not significantly different when mice were running in the track with or without objects (ØT: 6.79 ± 0.12 Hz, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: 6.59 ± 0.33 Hz, n = 8 sessions in two mice; Z = 1.26, p=0.20, two-tailed WRS test) but was lower than that reported for mice navigating in real linear tracks (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and comparison with literature.

claim: The power of theta oscillation was not significantly different between ØT and OT.
source: The power of theta oscillation (theta index see Materials and methods section) was also not significantly different (ØT: 3.31 ± 0.23, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: 3.38 ± 0.16, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t15 = 0.26, p=0.79, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Theta frequency was not modulated by running speed of the animal in ØT.
source: Theta frequency was not modulated by running speed of the animal in ØT (r = 0.02 ± 0.02, n = 9 sessions in three mice; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C) as previously observed in virtual linear tracks when only distal cues are present (Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C, and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: Theta frequency-speed modulation was significant in OT.
source: Theta frequency-speed modulation was, however, significant in OT (r = 0.08 ± 0.03, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t15 = -1.44, p=0.17, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Theta amplitude was similarly modulated by running speed in both conditions.
source: Theta amplitude was similarly modulated by running speed in both conditions (ØT: r = 0.07 ± 0.03, n = 9 sessions in three mice; OT: r = 0.03 ± 0.02, n = 8 sessions in three mice; t15 = 0.08, p=0.43, two-tailed unpaired t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: The proportion of active putative pyramidal cells with significant theta modulation was not different between conditions.
source: The proportion of active putative pyramidal cells with significant theta modulation was not different between conditions (ØT: 92.24%, n = 361 active cells; OT: 91.97%, n = 299 active cells; χ2 = 0.01, df = 1, p=0.89, Chi-Square test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was not significantly different between conditions in terms of preferred phase.
source: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was also not significantly different between conditions in terms of preferred phase (ØT: 203.91°±2.6, n = 361 active cells; OT: 191.17°±2.87, n = 299 active cells; p=0.07, circular Kruskal-Wallis; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) and strength (mean resultant vector length ØT: 0.18 ± 0.006, n = 361 active cells; OT: 0.19 ± 0.009, n = 155 active cells; Z = −1.63, p=0.1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was not significantly different between conditions in terms of strength.
source: The coupling of spikes to theta oscillation was also not significantly different between conditions in terms of preferred phase (ØT: 203.91°±2.6, n = 361 active cells; OT: 191.17°±2.87, n = 299 active cells; p=0.07, circular Kruskal-Wallis; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B) and strength (mean resultant vector length ØT: 0.18 ± 0.006, n = 361 active cells; OT: 0.19 ± 0.009, n = 155 active cells; Z = −1.63, p=0.1, two-tailed WRS test; Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: The percentage of fields with significant and negative correlation between phase and position was high in the track with objects but low in the empty track.
source: The percentage of fields with significant (p<0.05) and negative correlation between phase and position (i.e. precessing fields) was high in the track with objects (40.22%), comparable to that observed in real linear tracks in mice but low in the empty track (7.46%; χ2 = 26.57, df = 1, p<10−6 compared to OT, Chi-Square test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The correlation between phase and position was significantly different from zero for place cells recorded in the track with objects but not for those recorded in the track without objects.
source: Accordingly, the correlation between phase and position was significantly different from zero for place cells recorded in the track with objects (r = −0.14 ± 0.018, n = 177 fields; p<10−14, one sample sign-test; Figure 7A and B) but not for those recorded in the track without objects (r = 0.15 ± 0.024, n = 15 fields; p=0.30, one sample sign-test; Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Phase precession slopes were negative and significantly different from 0 for cells recorded in the track with objects but not in the track without objects.
source: Moreover, phase precession slopes (calculated on normalized place field sizes) were negative and significantly different from 0 for cells recorded in the track with objects (−2.00 ± 0.17 rad/U, n = 177 fields; p<10−14, one sample sign-test; Figure 7C) but not in the track without objects (1.82 ± 0.44 rad/U, n = 15 fields; p=0.3, one sample sign-test; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Local visual cues are important for proper theta phase precession in the hippocampus.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that local visual cues are important for proper theta phase precession in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theta phase precession analysis.

claim: There was a strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance in the presence of virtual 3D objects but not otherwise.
source: Our analysis revealed a strong correlation between theta phase and physical distance in the presence of virtual 3D objects (OT: R = 0.39, n = 629 pairs in three mice; p<10−24, Pearson correlation; Figure 7E,F) but not otherwise (ØT: R = 0.21, n = 28 pairs in three mice; p=0.26, Pearson correlation; Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Local visual cues are important for temporal coding in the hippocampus beyond theta phase precession.
source: These results show that local visual cues are important for temporal coding in the hippocampus beyond theta phase precession.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theta timescale spike coordination analysis.

claim: Spatial coding resolution was increased in the presence of local visual cues through an increase in the proportion of spatially selective place cells among active cells and enhanced place fields' spatial selectivity and stability.
source: We found that spatial coding resolution was increased in the presence of local visual cues through an increase in the proportion of spatially selective place cells among active cells but also enhanced place fields' spatial selectivity and stability.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: The effects of local visual cues on spatial coding resolution were most prominent in the vicinity of local cues and dynamic upon their manipulations.
source: These effects were most prominent in the vicinity of local cues and dynamic upon their manipulations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: Local sensory cues proved to be important for temporal place cell coding such as theta phase precession and theta timescale spike coordination.
source: Local sensory cues also proved to be important for temporal place cell coding such as theta phase precession and theta timescale spike coordination.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: Spatial resolution can be improved by pooling information across neurons.
source: Spatial resolution can be improved by pooling information across neurons (Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Local visual cues could dramatically increase the number of place cells among active cells by a threefold factor.
source: We found that local visual cues could dramatically increase the number of place cells among active cells (by a threefold factor).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: An increase in the quantity/quality of sensory cues in an environment will enhance the number of place cells coding that environment according to sensory-based models.
source: Using sensory-based models of place cells activation (Hartley et al., 2000; Strösslin et al., 2005; Barry et al., 2006; Sheynikhovich et al., 2009) one can predict that an increase in the quantity/quality of sensory cues in an environment will enhance the number of place cells coding that environment (Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction based on models cited in the literature.

claim: Previous studies using local enrichment with multimodal sensory cues or real objects reported only weak or no effects on dorsal hippocampal cell activity.
source: However, previous studies using local enrichment with multimodal sensory cues or real objects reported only weak or no effects on dorsal hippocampal cell activity.
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings in the literature.

claim: One study recording in rats navigating between cue-rich and cue-poor parts of the same track reported no effect on the proportion of place cells or on the density of place fields.
source: One study recording in rats navigating between cue-rich and cue-poor parts of the same track reported no effect on the proportion of place cells or on the density of place fields. Furthermore, population vector analysis did not reveal a better disambiguation of nearby locations in the cue-rich part of the track compared to the cue-poor suggesting similar spatial coding resolution (Battaglia et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Battaglia et al., 2004.

claim: Other studies found no overall increase of place cells proportion in 2D environment containing real objects nor a specific bias for place cells to fire near the objects.
source: Other studies found no overall increase of place cells proportion in 2D environment containing real objects nor a specific bias for place cells to fire near the objects (Renaudineau et al., 2007; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: One possibility to explain the lack of recruitment of additional cells in previous studies could be a high recruitment rate of the dorsal hippocampus even in the 'cue poor' condition due to the presence of uncontrolled local cues.
source: One possibility to explain the lack of recruitment of additional cells in these studies could be a high recruitment rate of the dorsal hippocampus even in the 'cue poor' condition due to the presence of uncontrolled local cues (Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and supported by a citation.

claim: Studies so far have revealed an homogeneous allocation of place fields in space in a given environment.
source: However, studies so far have revealed an homogeneous allocation of place fields in space (Muller et al., 1987; Rich et al., 2014) in a given environment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The proportion of object-responsive cells is generally low in the dorsal hippocampus (between 6 and 8%).
source: However, the proportion of these cells is generally low in the dorsal hippocampus (between 6 and 8%) which is in line with the fact that places near real objects are not overrepresented at the population level.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The proportion of object-responsive cells may be underestimated and vary depending on the recording location along both the proximo-distal axis and radial axis.
